'''Macquarie Group Limited''' ({{IPAc-en|m|ə|ˈ|k|w|ɔr|i}}), more commonly known as '''Macquarie Bank''', is an Australian multinational [[investment banking]] and [[financial services]] group headquartered in [[Sydney]] and listed on the [[Australian Securities Exchange]].
The company employs more than 20,000 staff<ref name="2023 Full Year Results Presentation">{{cite report|url=https://www.macquarie.com/assets/macq/investor/results-and-presentations/2023/macquarie-group-fy23-presentation.pdf |website=Macquarie Investor Relations |publisher=Macquarie Group |title=FY23 Presentation |access-date=5 May 2023}}</ref> across four operating groups in 34 markets.<ref name="aboutmacquarie">{{cite web |title=About {{!}} Macquarie Group |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about.html |website=Macquarie |publisher=Macquarie Group |access-date=5 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

Macquarie's [[investment banking]] division is Australia's top-ranked [[mergers and acquisitions]] adviser with more than {{Currency|871 billion|AUD|passthrough=yes}} in assets under management<ref name="FY23" /> and is one of the world's largest [[Infrastructure asset management|infrastructure asset managers]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://realassets.ipe.com/infrastructure/top-50-infrastructure-investment-managers-2018/realassets.ipe.com/infrastructure/top-50-infrastructure-investment-managers-2018/10025380.fullarticle|title=Top 50 infrastructure investment managers 2018|work=IPE RA|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/company/macquarie-asset-management/general-public/insights/perspectives/macquarie-asset-management-tops-infrastructure-investors-100-largest-infrastructure-managers.html |title=Macquarie Asset Management tops Infrastructure Investor's 100 largest infrastructure managers |publisher=Infrastructure Investor}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gourntis |first=Kalliope report|url=https://www.roymorgan.com/findings/9618-wealth-report-press-release-july-2024|title='Roy Morgan Wealth Report|edition=July 2024|quote=Macquarie Bank has the wealthiest customers|date=9 July 2024|author=Michele Levine|publisher=Roy Morgan}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.brokernews.com.au/news/breaking-news/bank-with-the-wealthiest-customers-revealed-285117.aspx|title=Bank with the wealthiest customers revealed|date=11 July 2024|publisher=Australian Broker}}</ref>

==History==

===Hill Samuel Australia===
Macquarie was founded on 10 December 1969 as Hill Samuel Australia Limited (HSA), a subsidiary of the UK's [[Hill Samuel|Hill Samuel & Co. Limited]].<ref name="themonthly">{{Cite news|url=https://www.themonthly.com.au/issue/2007/july/1240964771/gideon-haigh/who-s-afraid-macquarie-bank|title=Who's afraid of Macquarie Bank?|last=|date=4 July 2007|newspaper=The Monthly|access-date=9 February 2017|language=en-gb}}</ref>

The group's logo is a stylised version of the [[holey dollar]], Australia's first coinage, which was designed by [[Governor Macquarie]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-05-27 |title=Macquarie and the Holey Dollar - Macquarie Bank Limited |url=http://www.macquarie.com.au/holey_dollar.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527181552/http://www.macquarie.com.au/holey_dollar.htm |archive-date=27 May 2013 |access-date=2023-07-29}}</ref>

Australian businessman [[Stan Owens]] compiled a proposal for Hill Samuel & Co. to establish an Australian subsidiary. After presenting his report in [[London]], Owens was offered the role of implementing it. He became executive chairman of Hill Samuel Australia and founded the company from offices at [[Gold Fields House]] in Sydney's [[Circular Quay]]. The company's first three employees were Stan Owens, Blair Hesketh and Geoff Hobson. Later Chris Castleman (on loan from the British parent) and Bill Clarke joined. David Clarke and Mark Johnson were introduced to HSA and became joint managing directors in 1971. Despite being given a four-year allowance by the British parent to turn a profit, HSA was profitable by the end of its first twelve months of trading.

In 1971, HSA secured Australia's biggest mandate at the time, a {{Currency|60 million|USD|passthrough=yes}} financing for corrugated iron manufacturer [[Lysaght (Australian company)|John Lysaght Australia]]. HSA expanded its presence in the Australian market, opening a [[Melbourne]] office in 1972, and a [[Brisbane]] office in 1975.

===Macquarie Bank===
The 1980s were marked by significant financial market deregulation in Australia, including the floating of the Australian dollar and the removal of restrictions on foreign banks. To capitalise on the opportunities offered by deregulation, HSA submitted a proposal for the formation of a new substantially Australian owned and controlled bank to be called Macquarie Bank Limited.<ref name="themonthly" /> Authority for HSA to become Macquarie Bank Limited (MBL) was received from the [[Paul Keating]], then [[Treasurer of Australia|Federal Treasurer]], on 28 February 1985, making it only the second private trading bank to be established in Australia in modern times.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.rba.gov.au/statistics/tables/hist-series-breaks.html|title=Historical Series Breaks|website=Reserve Bank of Australia|language=en-AU|access-date=9 February 2017}}</ref>

The bank continued to grow its activities in the 1980s. It became Australia's leading bullion trader, initiated 24-hour foreign exchange trading, commenced stockbroking and corporate leasing activities, opened offices in London and [[Munich]], expanded into funds management by establishing Australia's first cash management account and formed a new structured finance business which would grow to become one of the largest in the world.<ref name="themonthly" /> It also implemented the risk management framework which is credited for the organisation's long history of unbroken profitability. The framework ensured Macquarie was not materially exposed to the [[Black Monday (1987)|October 1987 global share market crash]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Shake, rattle and roll |last=Sykes |first=Trevor |date=1997-10-17 |url=https://www.afr.com/politics/shake-rattle-and-roll-19971017-jlcf5 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20251128233613/https://www.afr.com/politics/shake-rattle-and-roll-19971017-jlcf5 |archive-date=2025-11-28 |work=The Australian Financial Review| quote=Some banks were hardly exposed at all. Macquarie and BT Australia had not been big lenders to the corporate cowboys and emerged comparatively stronger.}}</ref>

In other initiatives, Macquarie established its philanthropic arm, the Macquarie Group Foundation, which has since contributed more than $A330 million to community organisations around the world, and established what has become one of Australia's largest corporate art collections, the Macquarie Group Collection.<ref name="Art">{{Cite web|url=https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/galleries/australian/partners-message/|title=Partner's message :: Australian :: Art Gallery NSW|website=www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au|access-date=9 February 2017|archive-date=27 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927180417/https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/galleries/australian/partners-message/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

On 29 July 1996, Macquarie Bank Limited listed on the [[Australian Securities Exchange]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.switzer.com.au/your-money/investment-advice/share-trading/feature/macquarie-how-the-mighty-have-changed/|title=Macquarie – how the mighty have changed - Share Trading {{!}} Switzer|website=www.switzer.com.au|access-date=11 February 2017}}</ref> By 30 October 1996, Macquarie had entered the ASX [[All Ordinaries Index]], with a market capitalisation of approximately A$1.3 billion and would grow to more than $35 billion in 2018<ref name="HY22">{{Cite report |date=30 September 2021|title=Macquarie Group Limited, 1H22 Interim Financial Report|url=https://www.macquarie.com/assets/macq/investor/results-and-presentations/2022/macquarie-group-hy22-interim-report.pdf}}</ref> to become one of Australia's largest listed companies.

Macquarie continued its overseas expansion during the early 1990s, opening offices in [[New York City|New York]], [[Hong Kong]], [[Singapore]] and [[Beijing]], while extending its Australian operations to [[Perth]] and the [[Gold Coast, Queensland|Gold Coast]]. Acquisitions during the decade included Boston Australia Limited, Security Pacific Australia and the investment banking arm of [[Bankers Trust|Bankers Trust Australia]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB9305145389416296|title=Macquarie Bank to Acquire Unit of Bankers Trust Australia|last=Newswires|first=Dow Jones|date=28 June 1999|newspaper=Wall Street Journal|access-date=9 February 2017|issn=0099-9660}}</ref>

In 1994, Macquarie began its infrastructure investment business with the underwriting and placement of publicly listed equity for the [[M2 Hills Motorway|Hills Motorway]] in Sydney.<ref name="themonthly" /> It has continued to grow these activities to become the world's leading infrastructure manager.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.willistowerswatson.com/en/insights/2017/07/Global-Alternatives-Survey-2017|title=Global Alternatives Survey 2017|website=Willis Towers Watson|language=en|access-date=18 August 2017}}</ref> During the decade, Macquarie also launched its private banking and residential mortgages businesses and established a number of real estate and investment trusts.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Strategy |first=Cascade |title=Strategy Study: The Macquarie Group Growth Study |url=https://www.cascade.app/strategy-factory/studies/macquarie-group-strategy-study |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=www.cascade.app |language=en}}</ref>

Macquarie continued to expand its Asia operations in the early 2000s with the opening of offices in [[Seoul]] and [[Tokyo]] in 2000, and through the acquisition of [[ING Group]]'s Asian cash equities business in March 2004.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://east.com.au/publications/banking-news/macquarie-snaps-up-ings-asian-equity-business|title=East & Partners {{!}} Macquarie snaps up ING's Asian equity business|website=east.com.au|language=en-US|access-date=9 February 2017|archive-date=11 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170211160801/http://east.com.au/publications/banking-news/macquarie-snaps-up-ings-asian-equity-business|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The decade was also marked by the global expansion of Macquarie's infrastructure business, with infrastructure investment funds established in Korea, China, Europe, Russia, India and the Middle East. On 16 December 2004, [[Macquarie Infrastructure Corporation]] began trading as Macquarie Infrastructure Company Trust on the [[New York Stock Exchange]] (NYSE:MIC).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://investor.shareholder.com/mic/releasedetail.cfm?ReleaseID=158508|title=Macquarie Infrastructure Company Reports 2004 Results (NYSE:MIC)|website=investor.shareholder.com|language=en|access-date=9 February 2017}}</ref>

Macquarie made a number of significant acquisitions, particularly in the US, in the later part of the 2000s. These included US energy marketing and trading company Cook Inlet Energy Supply, establishing Macquarie's physical natural gas trading business in the US, and [[Constellation Energy Group|Constellation Energy]]'s Houston-based downstream natural gas trading operations. As at 2018, Macquarie Group is the second largest physical gas trader in North America.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.afr.com/business/macquaries-world-part-2-american-dream-built-on-energy-and-infrastructure-20180223-h0wkwl|title=Macquarie's World Part 2: American dream built on energy and infrastructure|date=2018-02-26|work=Financial Review|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref>

Other acquisitions included UK gas supply company Corona Energy in August 2006 and, in 2009, independent energy advisory firm Tristone Global Capital Inc; specialist investment bank [[Fox-Pitt Kelton Cochran Caronia Waller]]; Canadian wealth management business Blackmont Capital Inc; the wholesale electricity trading business of US firm [[Integrys Energy Group|Integrys Energy]]; US-based fixed income fund manager Allegiance Investment Management; the equity derivatives and structured products business of German private bank [[Sal. Oppenheim]]; and [[Condor Ferries]] service between the UK, Channel Islands and France.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.coronaenergy.co.uk/about-corona-energy/our-heritage/|title=The Corona Energy journey :: Corona Energy|newspaper=Corona Energy|access-date=9 February 2017|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://dealbook.nytimes.com/2009/09/30/macquarie-to-buy-fox-pitt-kelton/?_r=0|title=Macquarie to Buy the Boutique Firm Fox-Pitt Kelton|date=30 September 2009 |access-date=9 February 2017|language=en}}</ref>

In 2005, Macquarie announced an unsolicited takeover bid for the [[London Stock Exchange]] valuing the company at £1.5 billion, a bid rejected by LSE management.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/2928002/LSE-rejects-derisory-Macquarie-bid.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/finance/2928002/LSE-rejects-derisory-Macquarie-bid.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=LSE rejects 'derisory' Macquarie bid|last=Muspratt|first=Caroline|newspaper=Telegraph.co.uk|access-date=9 February 2017|language=en}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

===Macquarie Group===
In July 2006, Macquarie announced its intention to restructure the ''Macquarie Group'' into a non-operating [[holding company]] (NOHC)<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2007/macquarie-bank-releases-explanatory-memorandum-for-restructure-of-macquarie-group.html |title=Macquarie Bank releases Explanatory Memorandum for restructure of Macquarie Group |location=Sydney |date=14 September 2007}}</ref> owning separate banking and non-banking groups so as to support continued growth across the Group's businesses, particularly internationally, whilst meeting the requirements of the [[Australian Prudential Regulation Authority]] (APRA). Establishment of Macquarie Group Limited as the NOHC was approved by the [[Federal Court of Australia|Federal Court]] in October 2007.<ref>{{Cite press release |url=http://www.asx.com.au/asxpdf/20071029/pdf/315ffm0k0hr7sy.pdf|title=Macquarie Bank Limited Received Final Australian Federal Court Approval for Restructure of ''Macquarie Group'' |date=29 October 2007 |website=Australian Securities Exchange}}</ref>

Also that year, Macquarie, via a deal in which it acquired [[Thames Water]], a private utility company responsible for public water supply and waste water treatment in the [[London]] region of the [[UK]], was found to have transferred to Thames Water £2bn of debt before selling its stake in the company. These disclosures followed scrutiny of the possible financial causes of Thames Water's extensive pollution of the [[River Thames]], and other rivers, with untreated sewage between 2012 and 2014, for which Thames Water was fined a record £20m.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.ft.com/content/61bd8f0a-9181-11e7-bdfa-eda243196c2c | work=[[The Financial Times]] | title=Macquarie 'transferred £2bn of debt' on to Thames Water's books | date=5 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-41152516 | work=[[BBC News]]| title=How Macquarie bank left Thames Water with extra £2bn debt | date=5 September 2017}}</ref> In response to criticism, Macquarie noted that during its tenure Thames Water invested more than £11 billion, or around £1 billion per year, more than twice that invested during the five-year period before privatisation in 1989.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.afr.com/business/banking-and-finance/macquarie-sells-stake-in-uks-biggest-water-firm-20170315-guydkp|title=Macquarie sells stake in UK's biggest water firm|date=2017-03-15|work=Australian Financial Review |access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref> The [[Lee Tunnel]] was commissioned in January 2010 and opened by [[Boris Johnson]], then [[Mayor of London]], in January 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Smith|first=Claire|date=2016-01-29|title=Boris Johnson officially opens the Lee Tunnel|url=https://www.geplus.co.uk/news/boris-johnson-officially-opens-the-lee-tunnel-29-01-2016/|access-date=2021-09-09|website=Ground Engineering|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Garrett|first=Amy Ashenden, Luke|date=2016-01-28|title=Boris Johnson opens new 'super sewer' Lee Tunnel|url=https://www.standard.co.uk/hp/front/boris-johnson-opens-new-super-sewer-lee-tunnel-a3167691.html|access-date=2021-09-09|website=[[Evening Standard]]|language=en}}</ref> The capital investment undertaken to London's water supply was the first major investment since the Victorian era. Debts in Thames Water had gone from £3.2bn to £10.5bn by the time Macquarie had sold its stake, whilst paying out £2.8bn in dividends to shareholders during their time in control.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Laville |first1=Sandra |last2=Leach |first2=Anna |last3=Garcia |first3=Carmen Aguilar |title=In charts: how privatisation drained Thames Water's coffers |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2023/jun/30/in-charts-how-privatisation-drained-thames-waters-coffers |access-date=30 June 2023 |publisher=The Guardian Media Group |date=30 June 2023}}</ref> 
While Macquarie, once called a "vampire kangaroo" by the UK press,<ref name="AFR">{{cite news |last1=van Leeuwen |first1=Hans |date=30 May 2024 |title=Thames Water's big stink: Is Macquarie to blame? |url=https://www.afr.com/companies/infrastructure/thames-water-s-big-stink-is-macquarie-to-blame-20240522-p5jfkk |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240529230945/https://www.afr.com/companies/infrastructure/thames-water-s-big-stink-is-macquarie-to-blame-20240522-p5jfkk |archive-date=2024-05-29 |access-date=2 June 2024 |work=Australian Financial Review}}</ref> pulled out of Thames Water, in August 2021, it bought a majority stake in [[Southern Water]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2021/aug/09/macquarie-wades-back-into-uk-with-majority-stake-in-southern-water |title=Macquarie wades back into UK with majority stake in Southern Water |last=Ambrose |first=Jillian |date=10 August 2021 |website=The Guardian |access-date=1 July 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-58147606 |title=Southern Water: Bank buys majority stake in water firm after record fine |date=9 August 2021 |website=BBC News |publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=1 July 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2021/macquarie-asset-management-agrees-to-acquire-majority-stake-in-southern-water.html |title=Macquarie Asset Management agrees to acquire majority stake in Southern Water |date=9 August 2021 |website=Macquarie |access-date=1 July 2023}}</ref> It invested £1.6 billion ($3.1 billion) in what has been described as the UK's second most fragile water business, which, in 2024, risked being hit by the collapse of the now heavily financially troubled Thames Water.<ref name=AFR/>

In 2010, Macquarie completed its then largest acquisition with the purchase of [[Delaware Investments]], a  US-based diversified asset management firm, from [[Lincoln National Corporation|Lincoln Financial Group]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB125065237765942259|title=Macquarie to Acquire Delaware Investments|last=McFarland|first=Lyndal|date=20 August 2009|newspaper=[[Wall Street Journal]]|access-date=9 February 2017|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> As a result of the acquisition, Macquarie became one of the world's largest 50 asset managers.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.afr.com/business/banking-and-finance/financial-services/macquarie-tops-list-of-australias-largest-fund-managers-enters-worlds-top-50-20151102-gkopex|title=Macquarie tops list of Australia's largest fund managers, enters world's top 50|date=2015-11-02|work=[[Australian Financial Review]]|access-date=2018-07-02|language=en-US}}</ref> The same year, the company, through its subsidiary Macquarie Equipment Rentals, was criticised by the [[Australian Competition & Consumer Commission]] for suing 300 small businesses caught up in misleading telephony bundling deals.<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.smh.com.au/business/samuel-slams-macquarie-over-telco-scam-20101101-1799l.html | work=[[Sydney Morning Herald]] | title=Samuel slams Macquarie over telco scam | date=1 November 2010}}</ref>

[[File:General Post Office, Sydney.jpg|thumb|300x300px|[[General Post Office, Sydney|No. 1 Martin Place]], one of Macquarie Group's offices in [[Sydney]]]]
In March 2012, Macquarie acquired the buildings located at [[State Savings Bank Building|48–50 Martin Place]] and 9–19 Elizabeth Street from the [[Commonwealth Bank]] in preparation of their lease at current [[General Post Office, Sydney|No. 1 Martin Place]] offices expiring in 2024.<ref>{{cite press release|url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2021/macquarie-enters-into-agreement-for-sale-of-39-martin-place.html |title=Macquarie enters agreement to acquire 48 Martin Place |author=<!--Not stated--> |publisher=Macquarie Group |date=29 March 2012}}</ref>

In March 2014, the Private Equity Funds Management division — Macquarie Investment Management Private Markets (MIMPM) — was sold off to the former fund managers becoming ROC Equity Partners.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.afr.com/companies/macquarie-sells-private-equity-unit-20140318-ixdas|title=Macquarie sells private equity unit|date=18 Mar 2014|publisher=Australian Financial Review}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.moneymanagement.com.au/macquarie-sell-private-equity-funds-business|title=Macquarie to sell private equity funds business|date=18 Mar 2014|publisher=Money Management}}</ref> In October 2014, Macquarie joins the Global Infrastructure Facility (GIF), formed as part of an initiative by the [[World Bank Group]] conceived under Australia's G20 2014 presidency,<ref>{{cite AV media |title=World Bank Group Launches New Global Infrastructure Facility |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/video/2014/10/09/global-infrastructure-facility |date=9 October 2014 |publisher=World Bank Group}}</ref> as an advisory partner to share market insight, advice and expertise with the GIF and its government partners.<ref>{{cite press release |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2014/macquarie-group-joins-the-world-banks-global-infrastructure-facility.html |title=Macquarie Group joins the World Bank's Global Infrastructure Facility |author=<!--Not stated--> |publisher=Macquarie Group Limited |location=Washington D.C. |date=9 October 2014}}</ref>

In March 2015, Macquarie announced the acquisition of a US$4 billion aircraft operating lease portfolio from [[AWAS (company)|AWAS Aviation Capital]], bringing Macquarie's portfolio up to more than 220 aeroplanes.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-03-03/macquarie-to-buy-90-aircraft-for-4-billion-will-raise-capital|title=Macquarie to Buy Aircraft for $4 Billion, Raise Capital|date=3 March 2015|newspaper=[[Bloomberg News]]|access-date=9 February 2017}}</ref> In October Macquarie entered into an agreement to acquire the A$8.2 billion [[Esanda]] dealer finance portfolio from the [[ANZ Bank]].<ref>{{Cite press release |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2015/macquarie-esanda-and-outlook-update.html|title=Acquisition of Esanda dealer finance portfolio from ANZ Banking Group Limited, capital raising and update to short term outlook|website=www.macquarie.com|language=en|access-date=1 April 2021}}</ref>

In June 2017, Macquarie's Commodities and Global Markets business completed its acquisition of [[Cargill]]'s petroleum business as well as its North America power and gas business. ==Structure==
Macquarie has a non-hierarchical organisational structure where individual business entities are managed under four principal operating groups. These businesses work closely together, specialising in defined products or markets. There are also four shared services groups that provide the framework, infrastructure and support to the principal businesses.

===Annuity-style businesses===
Macquarie's annuity-style businesses consists of Macquarie Asset Management (formerly Macquarie Funds), Corporate and Asset Finance and Banking and Financial Services.
* '''Macquarie Asset Management''' (MAM) – is the world's biggest infrastructure asset manager and a top 50 global asset manager, managing more than $735.5 billion of asset on behalf of investors across multiple asset classes globally.
* '''Banking and Financial Services''' (BFS) – is Macquarie's retail bank offering personal banking, wealth management and business banking products and services to approximately 1.7 million clients, advisers, brokers and business clients.

===Capital markets facing businesses===
Capital Markets facing activities are undertaken by Macquarie Capital (formerly Investment Banking Group) and most businesses in Commodities and Global Markets, which was formed after the merger of Macquarie Securities Group (merger of Macquarie Capital Securities and the Macquarie Equity Markets Group),<ref>{{cite press release |date=2 June 2008 |title=Macquarie combines securities businesses to form Macquarie Securities |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2008/macquarie-combines-securities-businesses-to-form-macquarie-securities.html |location=Sydney |publisher=Macquarie Bank |access-date=2024-07-12}}</ref> and the Commodities and Financial Markets Group (formerly Fixed Income, Currencies and Commodities).<ref>{{cite press release |date=29 November 2016 |title=Macquarie Group merges Macquarie Securities Group and Commodities and Financial Markets Group |url=https://www.macquarie.com/au/en/about/news/2016/msg-cfm-merge.html |location=Sydney |publisher=Macquarie Bank |access-date=2024-07-12}}</ref>
* '''Macquarie Capital''' (MacCap) – advises companies on growth opportunities, sources investment funds, negotiates transactions and lists companies on the share market, as well as investing alongside clients.
* '''Commodities and Global Markets''' (CGM) – is a global business offering capital and financing, risk management, market access, physical execution and logistics solutions to its diverse client base.

===Central services groups===
Macquarie has a network of support groups that provide a range of functions supporting the principal Operating Groups, ensuring they have the appropriate workplace support and systems to operate effectively and the necessary resources to meet their regulatory, compliance, financial, legal and risk management requirements.
* '''Corporate Operations Group''' (COG) – provides specialist services under divisions that include technology, digital transformation and data, operations, human resources, business services/workplace, data, digital, corporate strategy, operational risk management, business resilience and global security, and the Macquarie Group Foundation.
* '''Financial Management Group''' (FMG) – is the financial hub of Macquarie focused on managing Macquarie's funding and capital. It provides strategic capital, tax and financial analysis and advice to senior management to support the growth of Macquarie's businesses around the world. It ensures Macquarie continues to meet its financial, regulatory and tax reporting compliance obligations in the jurisdictions in which Macquarie operates, and maintains relationships on behalf of the Group with a wide range of stakeholders such as regulators, partners, communities and shareholders.
* '''Legal and Governance Group''' (LGG) – brings together Macquarie's global team of dedicated lawyers, governance professionals, and the technical specialists, management, legal operations, and administrative staff who work with them.
* '''Risk Management Group''' (RMG) – forms the second line of defence and provides independent and objective review and challenge, oversight, monitoring and reporting in relation to Macquarie's material risks. Divisions include Compliance, Credit, Financial Crime Risk, Internal Audit, Market Risk, Operational Risk, Prudential Risk, and Central Risk.

===Licences===
Macquarie holds a number of licences enabling it to conduct activities in the jurisdictions in which it operates and is regulated by a significant number of regulators globally. In Australia, Macquarie Bank Limited holds a banking licence and as an [[authorised deposit-taking institution]] (ADI), is supervised by the [[Australian Prudential Regulation Authority]] (APRA). Other key Australian regulators include the [[Australian Securities & Investments Commission]] (ASIC) and [[AUSTRAC]]. Globally, key regulators include the UK [[Financial Conduct Authority|FCA]] and [[Prudential Regulation Authority (United Kingdom)|PRA]]; US [[Commodity Futures Trading Commission|CFTC]], [[Financial Industry Regulatory Authority|FINRA]], [[National Futures Association|NFA]], [[Federal Energy Regulatory Commission|FERC]], [[U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission|SEC]] and [[Federal Reserve System|Federal Reserve]] Board; [[Investment Industry Regulatory Organization of Canada|IIROC]]; [[Monetary Authority of Singapore|MAS]]; Hong Kong [[Securities and Futures Commission|SFC]]; [[Hong Kong Monetary Authority|HKMA]]; [[Securities and Exchange Board of India|SEBI]]; Japan [[Financial Services Agency|FSA]]; Korean [[Financial Supervisory Service (South Korea)|FSS]]; and New Zealand [[Financial Markets Authority (New Zealand)|FMA]].

==Regulatory breaches==
===2013 enforceable undertaking===
In January 2013 ASIC accepted an Enforceable Undertaking (EU) from Macquarie Equities Limited (MEL), part of Macquarie Group, after identifying widespread failures in its financial advice arm, Macquarie Private Wealth (MPW).<ref>{{cite web | title=13-010MR ASIC accepts enforceable undertaking from Macquarie Equities Ltd | url=https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2013-releases/13-010mr-asic-accepts-enforceable-undertaking-from-macquarie-equities-ltd/ }}</ref>

ASIC’s surveillance, starting in December 2011, uncovered serious and recurring compliance issues dating back to 2008. These included:
* Client files not containing statements of advice
* Advisers failing to demonstrate reasonable basis for advice provided to the client
* Poor client records and lack of detail contained in advice documents
* A lack of supporting documentation on files to determine if there was a reasonable basis for the advice provided to the client, and
* Failing to provide sufficient evidence that clients were sophisticated investors.

ASIC noted that MEL had been aware of these deficiencies for years but had failed to implement effective or timely remediation. As a result, ASIC required MEL to address systemic compliance failures that posed risks to consumers and market integrity.

===2021 breaches of prudential and reporting standards===
In April 2021 the [[Australian Prudential Regulation Authority]] (APRA) found that Macquarie Bank incorrectly treated certain intra‑group funding arrangements when calculating its [[Capital Requirement]] and related entity exposure metrics. It also breached [[Liquidity regulation|liquidity]] reporting standards between 2018 and 2020. This raised serious concerns about the bank’s risk‑management and reporting practices.<ref>{{cite web | title=APRA takes action against Macquarie Bank over multiple breaches of prudential and reporting standards | APRA | url=https://www.apra.gov.au/news-and-publications/apra-takes-action-against-macquarie-bank-over-multiple-breaches-of-prudential }}</ref> As a result, APRA imposed additional requirements on Macquarie Bank:

* An “operational capital overlay” of AUD 500 million to address operational risk stemming from its intra‑group structure. 
* A 15% add‑on to the net cash outflow component of its [[Liquidity ratio]] (LCR) calculation. 
* A 1% adjustment to the Available Stable Funding component of its [[Net stable funding ratio]] (NSFR) calculation.

APRA’s Deputy Chair, John Lonsdale, emphasised the importance of legally‑binding prudential and reporting standards, stating that the nature of the breaches by a major institution like Macquarie is “disappointing and unacceptable”.

===2025 OTC derivatives and futures compliance breach===

In May 2025 ASIC imposed additional licence conditions on Macquarie Bank after repeated and long‑standing compliance failures in its [[Futures contract|futures dealing]] business and [[Over-the-counter (finance)|OTC Derivatives]] trade reporting.<ref>{{cite web | title=25-068MR ASIC acts against Macquarie Bank for repeated compliance failures | url=https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2025-releases/25-068mr-asic-acts-against-macquarie-bank-for-repeated-compliance-failures/ }}</ref>
Key failures reported by ASIC included:
* Misreporting of more than 375,000 OTC derivative transactions, some for years without detection.
* Failure to prevent suspicious orders in the electricity futures market shortly after being fined nearly $5 million by ASIC’s Markets Disciplinary Panel. 
* Weak internal controls: poor change‑management, unclear roles, incomplete process knowledge and data‑governance issues.

ASIC’s Commissioner, Simone Constant, emphasised the recurrent nature of the failures and the need for sustainable, not “band‑aid”, fixes.

extract:
Macquarie Group Limited (), more commonly known as Macquarie Bank, is an Australian multinational investment banking and financial services group headquartered in Sydney and listed on the Australian Securities Exchange.
The company employs more than 20,000 staff across four operating groups in 34 markets.
Macquarie's investment banking division is Australia's top-ranked mergers and acquisitions adviser with more than A$871 billion in assets under management and is one of the world's largest infrastructure asset managers. Macquarie Bank's customers have an overall net wealth per capita of A$943,000 (as of March 2024), making them amongst the wealthiest in Australia.
